out: Explain serverless, microservices and Infrastructure as Code.
Identify when on-premises, OT or air-gapped designs apply.
plain: Choosing an architecture is like choosing where to live. Owning a house gives control but you fix the roof yourself. Renting an apartment means someone else handles the building, but you share walls. A hotel handles nearly everything, and you only bring your luggage.
tech: On-premises infrastructure is owned and run by the organization, giving maximum control and full responsibility. Cloud deployment models include public (shared provider infrastructure), private (dedicated to one organization), community (shared by organizations with common needs) and hybrid (a mix connected together). Multicloud means using more than one cloud provider, which reduces dependence on one vendor but increases complexity.

In serverless computing, the provider runs the servers and the customer supplies functions that run on demand, so the customer has no OS to patch but must still secure code, permissions and data. Microservices split an application into small independent services communicating through APIs, which limits the damage from one failure but adds many more connections to protect. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) defines infrastructure in version-controlled files, giving repeatable builds, but a single flawed template can replicate an error everywhere.

Operational technology (OT) controls physical equipment. An air-gapped network has no connection to outside networks, which is a strong control but can be defeated through removable media. Logical segmentation separates traffic using software such as VLANs and firewall rules. Physical segmentation uses separate hardware and cabling, which is stronger but costlier.
terms: Computing resources delivered on demand over a network.
Using more than one cloud provider.
The ways a cloud is provided: public, private, community and hybrid.
A combination of cloud and on-premises or different clouds.
A cloud shared among many customers.
A cloud shared by organizations with common needs.
Operational technology: systems controlling physical equipment.
Systems owned and run at the organization's own site.
A network with no connection to outside networks.
An application built as small services communicating over APIs.
Separating traffic through software such as VLANs.
Virtual LAN: a logical network on shared switches.
eg: A retailer uses Infrastructure as Code and scans templates before deployment, so that a public storage setting is caught before it exists.
A power plant keeps its control network separate from office IT, and carefully controls USB devices.

walks.title: Pick an architecture
steps: Requirement: a seasonal application with unpredictable demand. Consider public cloud or serverless.
Requirement: strict control of industrial machinery. Keep it on OT networks, separated.

lessons.title: Architecture models: cloud, on-premises, serverless and more
lessons.why: Each architecture moves the attack surface and changes who is responsible. A control that made sense in one design can be meaningless in another.
lessons.scenario: A government contractor must share a system with three other agencies under the same compliance rules, and wants to split the cost. Which deployment model fits best?
lessons.answer: A community cloud, which serves organizations with shared requirements and shares the costs among them.

product: Architecture choices limit what a product can promise. Serverless and managed services change who patches what. On-premises deployments mean customers run old versions for years, so a design must survive features being missing or out of date.

eng: Do all customers run the same version of this product?
sec: Which architecture decisions change our shared responsibility with customers?
prod: Which deployment options are we committed to supporting?

design.noex: The next lesson's exercise applies this knowledge to a concrete multi-tenant product.

plain: When buying a car, you weigh fuel, seats, price and who will service it. Choosing an architecture is the same, but the factors are availability, recovery, cost and legal requirements.
tech: Technical considerations: availability is uptime. Resilience is the ability to withstand failure and recover. Proprietary versus open source affects transparency, support and vendor dependence. Usability affects whether people follow secure paths. Responsibility defines who manages what. Compute is the processing capacity needed. Power requirements matter for dense or remote sites. Ease of recovery is how readily a system can be restored.

Business considerations: data sovereignty means data is subject to the laws of the country where it is stored. Data classification decides how strongly it must be protected. Cost includes both up-front capital and ongoing operating expenses. Ownership asks who is accountable for the system and its data. Environmental requirements cover temperature, humidity and physical conditions. Scalability is the ability to grow or shrink with demand. Risk is the overall exposure that the organization is willing to accept.
terms: How consistently a system is usable.
The ability to withstand and recover from disruption.
Closed vendor code compared with publicly available code.
How easily people can use something correctly.
Who is in charge of each security duty.
How readily a system can be restored.
Data being subject to the laws of where it is held.
Accountability for a system or its data.
Conditions a system needs, such as temperature.
The ability to grow or shrink capacity.
Overall exposure weighed in a decision.
eg: A European health company must keep patient data in the EU, so its cloud regions are chosen to meet that data sovereignty requirement.
A tool so awkward that staff bypass it has failed on usability, however strong it is on paper.

steps: List the options side by side.
List the factors that matter, such as availability, cost and sovereignty.
Weight each by importance to this organization.
Score the options and total them.
Write the recommendation and record the residual risk.

Score on-premises, public cloud and SaaS across eight considerations from this lesson.

labs.explain: The conclusion matters less than showing your reasoning. Real decisions depend on weighting.

lessons.title: Weighing architecture: technical and business considerations
lessons.why: There is no single best architecture. Security professionals advise on tradeoffs, and exam scenarios frequently ask which factor is driving a choice.
lessons.scenario: A Canadian company's contract says customer data must remain in Canada. A SaaS vendor stores data in several regions and cannot restrict it. Which consideration blocks this vendor?
lessons.answer: Data sovereignty and location requirements. Unless the vendor can guarantee Canadian storage, the contract cannot be met, whatever the vendor's other strengths.

product: In multi-tenant SaaS, many customers share one system, and the product's most important promise is that one customer can never reach another's data. Tenant switching, global search, shared caches and support tools are the places where that promise is most likely to break. Data residency turns an architecture decision into a setting and a sales conversation.

eng: At which layer are tenants isolated: application, database or infrastructure?
Which features query across tenants, including internal tools?
sec: How is tenant isolation tested, and how often?
prod: Which customers require a specific data region, and is that a contract term?

ex.title: Map tenant isolation and data residency
ex.scenario: A collaboration product serves companies in Canada, the EU and the US. A large customer asks where its data is stored and what stops another tenant seeing it. Users can also belong to more than one company's workspace.
ex.problem: The product has no clear model of tenant boundaries for users who belong to several tenants, and nothing tells administrators where their data lives.
tasks: Draw a data flow diagram for a document, from upload to search index, backup and third-party processors.
Mark where tenant boundaries and region boundaries are enforced.
Design the workspace switcher so a user always knows which tenant they are acting in.
Design the data residency panel, including what cannot be moved.
constraints: Cross-tenant data must never appear in search, autocomplete, notifications or caches.
Region promises must include backups and third-party processors.
Moving a tenant between regions may be slow, partial or impossible.
needs: Multi-tenant users need to avoid posting to the wrong company.
Customer administrators need accurate facts for their own compliance.
Sales needs claims that engineering can stand behind.
ex.deliver: A data flow diagram with boundaries marked, plus workspace switcher and residency panel designs.

crit.t: The diagram shows tenant and region boundaries, including backups and processors.
Wrong-tenant actions and cross-tenant leaks through search or notifications are addressed.
The active tenant is obvious at the moment a user takes an action.
Claims in the interface are checked against what engineering can actually guarantee.

seniors: Do not write a data promise into an interface until engineering and legal have confirmed it.
Note where isolation is a business decision too, because stronger isolation costs more and may be sold as a tier.

cq.s: Global search in a multi-tenant app shows matching document titles from every tenant, with content hidden until opened. What should a designer flag?

a.t: Titles are data, so limit results to the current tenant
a.w: Metadata can be sensitive, and it crosses the most important boundary here.

a.t: Results should be grouped alphabetically by tenant name
a.w: This improves the layout while leaving the leak in place.

a.t: Search should display fewer results on each page
a.w: Smaller pages still reveal other tenants' titles.

a.t: Titles are safe because the document body stays hidden
a.w: Titles can themselves reveal deals, patients or plans.

out: Place security devices and define security zones.
Describe the elements of Zero Trust architecture.
plain: Think of an airport. There is a public hall, a secure area after screening and restricted zones for staff. Guards stand at the transitions, not randomly in the middle of the hall.
tech: Device placement means putting each control where it can see or enforce the right traffic. A firewall sits at a boundary. An intrusion prevention system sits inline, while a detection sensor may watch a copy of traffic. Security zones group systems of similar trust and sensitivity, such as a screened subnet for public services, an internal zone and a restricted zone. Attack surface is reduced by removing exposure. Diversity means using different vendors, technologies or controls, so that one flaw does not defeat every layer.

In Zero Trust architecture, every request is evaluated. User authentication confirms who is asking, preferably with strong MFA. Device management checks device health, such as patch level and security software, and device inventory confirms that the device is known. Application access control grants access to specific applications, rather than to whole networks. The policy decision and enforcement functions apply these checks for each request.
terms: Positioning security tools where they can see or enforce traffic.
Network areas grouped by trust level.
A network area for public-facing services, separated from the internal network.
All the points where an attacker could get in.
Using different technologies or vendors to avoid shared weaknesses.
A design in which every request is evaluated regardless of network location.
Verifying who is making a request.
Keeping track of devices and their condition.
Whether a device meets security requirements such as patch level.
Granting access to specific applications instead of whole networks.
eg: A public web server sits in a screened subnet, so if it is compromised, a second firewall still separates it from internal databases.
A company uses a firewall from one vendor at the edge and another internally, so one vendor's flaw does not open both.

walks.title: Place controls for a small company
steps: Identify the zones: internet, screened subnet, users, servers.
Place a firewall at each boundary.
Put public services in the screened subnet.
Place an inline IPS where blocking is needed, and sensors where visibility is needed.
Allow only the required flows between zones and deny the rest.

labs.title: Design a segmented network
do: Draw a company with staff, guests, servers, a public website and a building-control system.
Assign each group to a zone and give each a subnet from 10.0.0.0/16.
Write the allowed flows between zones, with everything else denied.

Guest and building-control traffic is isolated from user and server zones.

qs.s: Where should a public-facing web server usually be placed?

a.w: This separates it from internal systems.
A compromise would then land among users.
This would expose control systems.

a.t: On the same subnet as the database
a.w: This removes a layer of separation.

qs.s: A security team wants a tool to stop malicious traffic automatically. Where must it be placed?

a.w: Only an inline device can block in real time.
A mirror only receives a copy of traffic.
It would see nothing.

qs.s: A managed laptop is out of date and fails a health check. What should a Zero Trust system do?

a.t: Deny or limit access until it is remediated
a.w: Device health is part of the access decision.

a.t: Grant full access because the password was correct
a.w: Authentication alone is not sufficient.

a.t: Grant access because the laptop is on the corporate network
a.w: Location gives no trust.
This is out of proportion.

qs.s: Why might an organization use firewalls from two vendors?

a.t: A vulnerability in one is less likely to affect the other
a.w: Diversity avoids a single shared weakness.

a.t: To eliminate the need to patch
a.w: Both still need patches.
They will differ in practice.

a.t: Because one firewall cannot enforce any rules
a.w: A single firewall can enforce rules.

Equating being inside the network with being trusted.
sum: Put controls where they can see or enforce traffic.
Zones limit how far an attacker can move.
Zero Trust checks user, device and application for each request.
cards: A network area for public services, separated from the internal network.
Why does an IPS have to be inline?
To block traffic, it must be in the traffic path.
lessons.title: Secure infrastructure: zones, placement and Zero Trust architecture
lessons.why: Where you put a control matters as much as which control you buy. An IDS watching the wrong link sees nothing, and a flat network lets a single compromise spread everywhere.
lessons.scenario: An organization has one flat network. Ransomware on a single laptop spreads to its servers within minutes. Which architectural change would most directly limit this?
lessons.answer: Segmentation into security zones with controlled traffic between them. Servers would be reachable only through the ports required, which limits lateral movement.

product: Zero Trust reaches users as continuous checks: a device must be compliant, a session can be re-evaluated, and access can change partway through. Interfaces need to explain why someone who was allowed a moment ago is now being blocked.

eng: Which signals can change a user's access during a session?
sec: Which zones or policies does this feature cross?
prod: How do customers configure these policies, and who gets the support call?

design.noex: The failure-mode exercise in the next lesson applies these ideas directly.

out: Choose remote access and secure communication options.
Prevent privilege creep and use service accounts safely.
Decide whether a device should fail open or fail closed.
plain: A VPN is a private corridor. Out-of-band management is a separate service entrance used when the main entrance is blocked. Failure modes ask: when the electronic lock loses power, does the door stay locked or open?
tech: Secure communication and access: a virtual private network (VPN) creates an encrypted path, and remote access lets users or admins reach systems from elsewhere. Tunneling encapsulates one protocol within another. User management controls accounts. User access should follow least privilege. End-to-end encrypted messaging means only the participants can decrypt content, not the service provider. Out-of-band management uses a separate path to manage devices, even if the main network is down. File transfer should use protected methods such as SFTP. Security Service Edge (SSE) delivers security functions from the cloud, including secure web gateway, cloud access security broker and Zero Trust network access.

Identity management: Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) are a Windows feature that automatically manage long, rotating passwords for services. Least privilege access accounts have only the rights required, with separate admin accounts for admin work. Privilege creep is the build-up of permissions as people change roles without old access being removed.

Failure modes describe how a device behaves when it fails. Fail-closed blocks traffic, favouring security over availability. Fail-open allows traffic through, favouring availability. Inline security devices are chosen deliberately, based on what the organization values more. Note that life-safety systems, such as emergency exits, must allow people out.
terms: An encrypted connection across another network (VPN).
What accounts are allowed to reach.
Messaging in which only participants hold the keys.
Managing devices through a separate path.
Moving files, which should be done with protected methods.
Cloud-delivered security for users and applications (SSE).
Group Managed Service Accounts: Windows service accounts with automatic password management.
Accounts limited to the rights required.
How a device behaves when it fails.
A device blocks traffic when it fails.
A device allows traffic when it fails.
eg: An IT staff member moves through three departments and retains access to all three. An access review finds this privilege creep.
A hospital's inline device fails open, so clinical systems stay reachable, and the alert prompts urgent attention.

walks.title: Choose a failure mode
steps: Ask which is worse: downtime or unfiltered traffic?
For a payment system firewall, fail-closed usually protects data.
For a device whose failure would stop clinical care, fail-open may be chosen.
Document the decision and make sure failure triggers an alert.

labs.title: Review account access
do: Run getent passwd and identify human accounts, usually with IDs of 1000 or more.
Run groups for each account you made, and check which accounts have sudo.
Remove sudo from an account that does not need it using sudo deluser labuser sudo, if it is a member.
Run sudo -l as that user to verify what it can do.
labs.expect: A list of accounts and privileges, and a confirmed reduction in access.
labs.explain: This is an access review in miniature. Regular reviews are what stop privilege creep.
pass: You verified that an unneeded privilege is gone.

qs.s: A firewall that blocks all traffic when it fails is said to do what?

a.w: It prioritizes security over availability.
That allows traffic through.
That is a change management term.
This means switching to a standby.

qs.s: An employee has retained access from three former roles. What is this?

a.w: Permissions have built up over time.
That is storing keys for recovery.
That is misleading an AI model.
That is a failure mode.

qs.s: Which feature helps with long, automatically rotated passwords for Windows services?

a.w: Group Managed Service Accounts automate password management.
That lists revoked certificates.
That is a monitoring protocol.
That is a recovery metric.

a.t: A separate path for administering devices
a.w: It stays available when the production network is not.

a.t: Sending management traffic over the normal user VLAN
a.w: This is in-band.
This is a data protection activity.

a.t: Encrypting a message end to end
a.w: This protects message content.

qs.s: What does Security Service Edge primarily deliver?

a.t: Cloud-delivered security for access to web, cloud and private applications
a.w: It includes functions such as ZTNA and secure web gateways.
This is a power function.

a.t: A physical mantrap for a data centre
a.w: This is physical security.
This belongs to PKI.

mistakes: Assuming a VPN grants appropriate access. It should still be limited by least privilege.
Treating fail-open as always wrong. It is a tradeoff to be decided deliberately.
sum: Protect remote paths with encryption and least privilege.
Review accounts to stop privilege creep.
cards: Accumulating more access over time, usually through role changes.
Fail-closed or fail-open: which favours availability?
lessons.title: Secure access, identity management and failure modes
lessons.why: Remote work made access paths a primary target. Accounts tend to accumulate access over time, and a device's behaviour during failure can quietly decide what happens when you need it most.
lessons.scenario: After a network outage, administrators cannot reach their switches to fix it, because management runs over the same failed network. What should have been in place?
lessons.answer: Out-of-band management, a separate path to device consoles such as a dedicated management network or cellular link.

product: Security controls fail, and when they do a product must either fail open and keep working unsafely, or fail closed and stop people working. That decision can appear as a login outage, a blocked payment or a safety-critical record that clinicians cannot open.

eng: What happens to signed-in sessions when the identity service is unavailable?
Can we tell the difference between a denial and a failed policy check?
sec: Which functions should fail closed, and which may degrade?
prod: What are our customers' obligations during an outage, such as patient care?

ex.title: Design what happens when the security system fails
ex.scenario: A hospital's scheduling and records application relies on a third-party identity and policy service. During a recent outage, nobody could sign in and staff could not view patient schedules.
ex.problem: The product has no designed behaviour for a failed identity or policy service, so it presents a generic error at the worst possible moment.
tasks: For each key function, decide whether it should fail open, fail closed or degrade, and explain why.
Design the degraded mode and how a user knows they are in it.
Design the break-glass route for emergency access, including after-the-fact review.
constraints: Emergency access must be logged, time-limited and reviewed.
Unknown states must never appear as granted permissions.
Data entered in degraded mode must be reconciled once service returns.
needs: Clinicians need critical information during an outage.
Privacy officers need a record of any emergency access.
Administrators need to know what is happening and for how long.
ex.deliver: A fail-open, fail-closed or degrade decision table, plus degraded mode and break-glass designs.

crit.t: Break-glass access is limited in time, logged and reviewed.
The decisions consider safety and privacy consequences for each function.
Users can tell they are in a degraded state and what is limited.
The decision table identifies who must approve each fail-open choice.

seniors: Fail-open decisions involve safety and legal judgment, so they need owners beyond the design team.
Rehearsing outages reveals assumptions, so ask to join a recovery exercise.

cq.s: A payment approval service is unreachable. Which behaviour is the best default for a large transfer?

a.t: Hold the transfer and tell the user what will happen
a.w: Failing closed protects integrity while keeping the person informed.

a.t: Approve it automatically and verify it later
a.w: Failing open on a high-value action invites irreversible loss.

a.t: Silently retry forever with no message to the user
a.w: The user is left guessing, and may submit the transfer twice.

a.t: Cancel it and delete all the details the user entered
a.w: This fails safely, but it needlessly destroys the user's work.
